cases.abstract: A larger context window does not necessarily let a language model use evidence wherever it appears. We examine this distinction through multi-document question answering and synthetic key-value retrieval, changing context length and the location of the relevant item while holding the required answer fixed. Question-answering accuracy is generally highest with evidence at either end and lower in the middle; some document-rich configurations perform worse than answering without documents. Extended-context models behave almost identically to their shorter-context counterparts when both can accommodate the input, separating capacity to accept text from ability to use it. Repeating the query before and after the context largely resolves synthetic lookup failures but leaves the question-answering position pattern substantially unchanged. Thus, making an exact match accessible does not establish effective use of natural-language evidence. Encoder-decoder models are relatively insensitive to position within their training-time context lengths but develop middle-context degradation beyond them. In a standard retrieval pipeline, reader accuracy saturates before retrieval recall. These comparisons identify effective evidence use, rather than nominal context capacity or evidence availability alone, as a limitation in the evaluated question-answering systems.
cases.methods: The diagnostic design separates evidence availability from the model's ability to use it at different locations. For 2,655 NaturalQuestions-Open queries with paragraph answers, prompts combine an annotated answer passage with relevant retrieved distractors filtered to exclude annotated answers. Moving the answer passage within a fixed document set changes its position without changing the answer or removing its support. Increasing the distractor count produces contexts of 10, 20, or 30 documents, testing the effect of additional material. Closed-book and single-passage oracle prompts establish references for memory-based answering and evidence use without distraction. A complementary task uses unique random UUID key-value pairs to reduce semantic confounds while retaining a designated lookup target. Both tasks use greedy decoding and count outputs containing a correct answer or value. Repeating the query before and after the data tests whether enabling query-aware contextualization changes exact lookup and question answering differently.
cases.results: Query placement distinguishes success at exact lookup from effective use of retrieved prose. With 300 UUID key-value pairs, GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K) reaches 100% accuracy when the query appears before and after the data, compared with a worst-position accuracy of 45.6% when the query only follows the data. The same intervention barely changes the question-answering position pattern: it slightly helps evidence at the beginning and slightly hurts other positions. The Claude-1.3 variants likewise achieve near-perfect synthetic retrieval while remaining position-sensitive in question answering. These contrasts show that repairing lookup does not resolve the broader evidence-use problem. In some 20- and 30-document configurations, GPT-3.5-Turbo falls below its 56.1% closed-book accuracy despite receiving an answer passage. Evidence availability therefore does not ensure a benefit when that passage is embedded among distractors. In the standard retrieval pipeline, reader accuracy gains become marginal beyond 20 documents even as recall continues improving, indicating that additional retrieved material is not being converted into corresponding answer gains.
cases.notes: Retained the diagnostic argument: accepting more text, finding an exact match, and using answer evidence are distinct capabilities. The abstract's shared-window contrast is supported by Section 2.3; its query-placement contrast by Section 4.2. Methods makes the fixed-answer intervention explicit (Sections 2.1 and 3.1). Results links lookup recovery to persistent QA sensitivity, rather than presenting it as a general fix (Sections 3.2 and 4.2), and retains the below-closed-book outcome (Section 2.3). Distractors exclude annotated answers, not every plausible answer. Architectural explanations remain hypotheses; the ambiguous decline described as exceeding 20% is omitted.

cases.abstract: Retrieval can supply relevant text without ensuring that a generated claim is supported by it. SELF-RAG addresses this mismatch by training a language model to request retrieval and assess passage relevance, evidential support, and response utility through reflection tokens. A critic trained on GPT-4 feedback annotates instruction-output pairs offline; the generator learns both text and evaluations with a standard next-token objective. At inference, it generates sentence continuations for retrieved passages and ranks them using generation probabilities and weighted self-evaluations. Selection can therefore favor continuations judged better supported rather than rely on passage relevance alone, with retrieval frequency and support emphasis adjustable without retraining. Llama 2 models with 7B and 13B parameters are evaluated zero-shot on six tasks. On ASQA, the 7B model achieves 66.9% citation precision versus 5.0% for Llama2-FT 7B, which uses the same instruction-output training pairs but adds retrieval only at inference; both receive the same five documents. However, str-em correctness is slightly lower, at 30.0% versus 31.0%. Increasing the support weight also improves citation precision while reducing MAUVE, exposing a tradeoff rather than uniform improvement.
cases.methods: SELF-RAG trains the generator to supply the judgments later used to select its own continuations, avoiding a separate critic call at inference. Offline, a Llama 2 critic distilled from GPT-4 feedback marks retrieval needs, passage relevance, support for each target segment, and overall response utility. The generator learns ordinary text and these reflection tokens together; retrieved passages remain conditioning context but are excluded from the training loss. At inference, each retrieved passage conditions a candidate sentence. Segment-level beam search scores candidates using generation probabilities plus weighted, normalized probabilities of favorable relevance, support, and utility tokens. A relevant passage can accompany a weakly supported continuation; scoring support separately lets decoding prefer continuations it judges better grounded. Changing these weights or the retrieval threshold alters decoding behavior without retraining, separating whether to obtain evidence from how strongly support should influence answer selection.
cases.results: SELF-RAG improves attribution without uniformly improving answer correctness. With the same five supplied ASQA passages, its 7B model attains 66.9% citation precision and 67.8% recall, compared with 5.0% and 7.5% for Llama2-FT 7B. Both use the same 150,000 instruction-output pairs, but the baseline adds retrieval only at inference and lacks reflective training. Yet SELF-RAG's str-em correctness is 30.0%, below the baseline's 31.0%. The contrast supports better evidence attribution rather than a gain on every answer metric. In the 50,000-example training ablation, evaluated on 150 sampled ASQA questions, training with the top retrieved passage but no reflection tokens reduces str-em from 32.1% to 18.1%. This comparison supports the combined training configuration, not an isolated effect of one token. Increasing the support weight at inference improves citation precision but lowers MAUVE; raising the retrieval threshold reduces retrieval frequency and hurts PopQA accuracy more than PubHealth accuracy. These tradeoffs make the preferred configuration dependent on the task and evaluation objective.
cases.notes: Preserved evidence selection and inference-time control as complementary contributions. The abstract connects critique-weighted ranking to support beyond relevance (Sections 3.1 and 3.3), then pairs citation gains with the lower ASQA str-em score (Table 2). Methods explains how offline annotations become generator-produced selection scores (Sections 3.2-3.3). Results distinguishes the 150,000-pair main comparison from the 50,000-example, 150-question ASQA ablation (Section 5.2). The no-critic variant also changes passage handling, so its loss is not assigned to a single token. Greater support weight improves citation precision but lowers MAUVE; neither metric nor the learned critique tokens guarantees complete support.
